meta.label: Field Hockey
meta.indoorOutdoor: outdoor (water-based or sand-based artificial turf); indoor variant exists
meta.contactLevel: low-moderate (stick/ball impacts, incidental body contact; no tackling through the player)
meta.competitionFrequencyPerWeek: 1 match/week typical (club); congested weekends and tournaments (2-4 matches in 2-5 days) at representative level
meta.notes: Four 15-minute quarters with rolling substitutions — interchange keeps on-pitch intensity high. The semi-crouched playing posture (ball on a short stick) is the sport's defining orthopaedic demand: sustained hip/trunk flexion under running load.

maxStrength.why: Underpins acceleration, hitting power and tissue robustness, but hockey is not strength-limited; relative strength matters more than absolute.
maxStrength.source: Suchomel 2016 (strength as a foundation for athletic performance)

relativeStrength.why: Strength-to-bodyweight drives the game's constant accelerations, decelerations and lunging reaches.

explosivePower.why: First-step acceleration, hitting/slapping velocity and the drag-flick all express rapid force; interchange play rewards repeated explosive efforts.
explosivePower.source: López de Subijana 2010 (drag-flick biomechanics); expert consensus

reactiveStrength.why: Quick ground contacts in COD and re-acceleration on low-compliance turf; lower jumping demand than aerial sports.

sprintSpeed.why: Breakaways and defensive recovery runs reach high speed, though pitch size and structure cap maximal-velocity exposure vs football codes.

acceleration.why: The dominant locomotor action: repeated 5-20 m bursts to press, lead, track and re-position — most efforts never reach top speed.
acceleration.source: Spencer et al. 2004 (time-motion, repeated sprints); McGuinness et al. 2019 (women's international GPS)

deceleration.why: Stopping into tackles, closing down and re-cutting from the crouched position; eccentric capacity protects knee/hamstring.

changeOfDirection.why: Elimination skills, pressing angles and marking all pivot on sharp COD executed from a low body position.

aerobicEndurance.why: ~5-9 km per match (position-dependent) at high mean intensity; aerobic fitness drives repeat-effort recovery and late-quarter output.

anaerobicEndurance.why: Rolling substitutions let players work in repeated near-maximal blocks — glycolytic tolerance shapes shift quality.

repeatSprintAbility.why: The defining fitness quality: clusters of maximal sprints with incomplete recovery, especially in pressing structures.
repeatSprintAbility.source: Spencer et al. 2004 (repeated-sprint activity in field hockey)

mobility.why: Hip flexion/rotation range and hamstring extensibility make the low playing position sustainable and protect the lumbar spine.
mobility.source: expert consensus; low-back demand literature (Reilly & Seaton 1990)

stability.why: Lumbopelvic control under sustained trunk flexion is hockey's signature demand; single-leg control for lunging reaches and COD.
stability.source: Reilly & Seaton 1990 (spinal loading in hockey); expert consensus

rotationalPower.why: Hitting, slapping and the drag-flick transfer force through hip-trunk rotation from a flexed base.
rotationalPower.source: López de Subijana 2010 (drag-flick kinematics); expert consensus

gripStrength.why: Stick control under contact and repeated hitting need forearm endurance more than maximal grip.

neckStrength.why: Low head-contact exposure (ball-strike risk is managed by rules/equipment, not trainable neck strength).

balance.why: Reaching tackles and eliminations on one leg from a low base; balance underpins the lunge-heavy defensive game.

coordination.why: Stick-and-ball control at speed in a bent posture is a high coordinative load; gym work must not blunt it with fatigue.

energySystems.workToRestRatio: ~1:3 to 1:5 on-pitch (intermittent bursts within continuous play); interchange adds bench recovery between high-intensity shifts
energySystems.matchDemands: ~5-9 km total (position + interchange dependent); high-speed running ~400-900 m; sprint efforts commonly 5-20 m; hundreds of accelerations/decelerations; sustained semi-crouched posture throughout
energySystems.heartRateProfile: Mean ~80-85% HRmax on pitch; repeated periods >90% HRmax during presses and penalty-corner sequences
energySystems.fatigueProfile: High-intensity running declines across quarters without interchange management; trunk-position quality degrades with fatigue — a low-back and skill-execution risk
energySystems.source: Lythe & Kilding 2011; McGuinness et al. 2019; Spencer et al. 2004
energySystems.notes: Elite figures from international GPS/HR studies; club demands are lower in volume but similar in pattern. Quarters (2015 rule change) raised on-pitch intensity vs older halves-based studies.

primaryPatterns: change of direction from a low base
movementProfile.jointLoading: High cumulative hip/knee eccentric load from deceleration and COD; sustained lumbar flexion under load is the sport's signature stress; ankle inversion exposure on turf
movementProfile.groundContacts: Very many sub-maximal high-frequency contacts; moderate maximal-velocity exposure; artificial turf is fast with high grip (loads ankle/knee on cuts)
movementProfile.landingDemands: Low-moderate — minimal jumping; occasional aerial receives and GK dives
movementProfile.throwing: None overhead; all striking actions are stick-mediated from a flexed, rotating base
movementProfile.jumping: Low for outfield players (occasional aerial control); high and reactive for goalkeepers (dives, splits)
movementProfile.cutting: Constant — eliminations, pressing angles, re-marking; usually initiated from the semi-crouched position
movementProfile.rotating: High — every hit, slap, sweep and drag-flick rotates hip-to-shoulder over a planted base
movementProfile.overheadActions: Rare (aerial pass receipt); not a programming priority
movementProfile.collisions: Low-moderate incidental contact; stick/ball impact injuries are equipment/rules-managed, not gym-trainable
movementProfile.repeatedImpacts: Repetitive footstrike on artificial turf; cumulative lower-limb tendon + calf load
movementProfile.asymmetricLoading: Strongly asymmetric: hockey is played right-handed only (rules), so the left side leads the crouch and rotation — left-hip/trunk bias and one-sided lunging patterns are near-universal
commonDeficiencies: posterior-chain endurance vs the crouched posture (low-back overload)
adductor strength vs lunging volume (groin overload)
left-right asymmetry from the one-sided playing position

common.name: Hamstring strain
common.mechanism: repeated acceleration/deceleration and lunging reach at speed

modifiable: restricted hip mobility loading the posterior chain

common.rtpConsiderations: Progressive sprint reloading + eccentric strength restoration; test at match-intensity accelerations before return.
common.source: field-hockey injury surveillance (Theilen 2016; Rees 2020 review); van Dyk 2019

common.name: Low-back pain (extensor overload)
common.mechanism: sustained semi-crouched posture under running load; repeated flexed-base rotation (hitting, flicking)
common.rtpConsiderations: Restore pain-free hip hinge + trunk endurance before reintroducing high hitting/flick volumes; manage drag-flick reps like sprint reps.
common.source: Reilly & Seaton 1990 (spinal loading in hockey); hockey surveillance reviews (Rees 2020)

common.name: Ankle sprain (lateral)
common.mechanism: cutting and pressing on high-grip artificial turf; contested-ball stances
common.rtpConsiderations: Graded COD re-exposure + balance retraining; taping/bracing on return is evidence-supported.

common.name: Groin/adductor strain
common.mechanism: lunging tackles and low lateral reaches; repeated adduction under stretch from the crouched base
common.rtpConsiderations: Copenhagen-based strength restoration; progress lunging/COD volume gradually; monitor squeeze strength.

common.name: Knee ligament injury (ACL/MCL)
common.incidence: lower than football codes but present — elevated in the women's game
common.mechanism: plant-and-cut on high-grip turf; deceleration into the lunge

nonModifiable: female sex (2-4x relative risk in cutting sports)

common.rtpConsiderations: Criteria-based RTP; strength symmetry + hop batteries + on-turf COD progression.
common.source: ACL prevention meta-analyses (Webster & Hewett 2018); hockey surveillance

common.name: Calf/Achilles overload
common.mechanism: high-frequency turf running + constant ankle stiffness demand in the crouched gait
common.rtpConsiderations: Isometric → heavy-slow-resistance calf progression; keep pitch exposure graded.

injuryProfile.summary: Hamstring, groin and ankle mirror other field sports; the differentiators are LOW-BACK overload from the crouched playing posture and pronounced LEFT-RIGHT asymmetry from the one-sided stick — both are directly addressable in the gym.

positions.name: Goalkeeper
positions.role: Shot-stopping in full protective kit; commanding the circle; distribution.
positions.movementDemands: Low total distance; explosive lateral pushes, splits, dives and rapid recoveries under ~20 kg of kit.
positions.powerReq: high (explosive push-off + recovery from the ground)
positions.bodyComposition: Reactive and mobile; leaner aids repeated floor work.
positions.recoveryConsiderations: Low running load — tolerates more gym; manage hip/groin soreness from repeated splits.

positions.name: Defender
positions.role: Circle defence, marking, outletting; often first receiver under press.
positions.movementDemands: Positional discipline with repeated short accelerations, lunging tackles and low blocks; frequent hitting (long outlets).
positions.runningDemands: Moderate total distance; high deceleration + lunge counts.
positions.bodyComposition: Stronger builds tolerated; movement quality still decisive.
positions.recoveryConsiderations: Hitting/outlet volume loads the trunk — watch low-back soreness after high-hit sessions.

positions.name: Midfielder
positions.role: Link play; the largest running load; press triggers and recovery runs.
positions.movementDemands: Continuous box-to-box shuttling in the crouched carry position; constant accelerations.
positions.runningDemands: Highest total + high-speed distance (~8-9 km elite).
gymPriorities: minimal-dose strength that never blunts running quality
positions.recoveryConsiderations: Highest weekly running load — gym volume must flex around pitch load, never compound it.

positions.name: Forward
positions.role: Pressing from the front; elimination 1v1s; circle finishing and deflections.
positions.movementDemands: Sprint-press clusters, sharp eliminations from a deep crouch, deflection stances.
positions.runningDemands: High sprint counts; moderate-high total distance.
positions.recoveryConsiderations: Sprint-density days need 48 h before heavy posterior-chain gym work.

assessments.name: Countermovement jump (CMJ)
assessments.purpose: Lower-body power + neuromuscular fatigue monitoring (drop vs rolling baseline).

assessments.name: 10 m / 40 m sprint
assessments.purpose: Acceleration (10 m) is the game's dominant action; 40 m captures the rarer top-speed exposures.

assessments.name: 30-15 Intermittent Fitness Test
assessments.purpose: Intermittent aerobic capacity that maps directly onto interchange-based conditioning prescription.

assessments.name: Repeated-sprint ability (6×30 m, 20 s)
assessments.purpose: The defining match quality — sprint decrement under incomplete recovery.

assessments.name: Nordic hamstring strength
assessments.purpose: Eccentric hamstring strength — the headline modifiable hamstring-injury factor.
assessments.frequency: each block + after any hamstring flag

assessments.name: Adductor squeeze (45°)
assessments.purpose: Groin capacity + weekly early-warning monitor for the lunge-heavy game.

assessments.name: Trap-bar deadlift (3-5RM est.)
assessments.purpose: Global lower-body strength anchor; safe hinge under load mirrors the playing posture done WELL.

assessments.name: Single-leg calf raise capacity
assessments.purpose: Calf strength-endurance vs turf running load; Achilles overload screen.

assessments.name: Hip mobility screen (flexion + internal rotation)
assessments.purpose: Hip range that keeps the crouch out of the lumbar spine; asymmetry flags the one-sided posture.

youth.trainingEmphasis: Athletic literacy first; the crouched skill posture is trained on pitch — the gym builds the hips and trunk that make it sustainable.
commonMistakes: specialising the drag-flick young (lumbar growth-plate risk)
ignoring left-right asymmetry from day one

development.trainingEmphasis: Build the tissue capacity the senior game will tax: hips, hamstrings, adductors, trunk endurance.
commonMistakes: skipping the strength base for skills-only development

highest: strength maintenance at minimal effective dose
senior.trainingEmphasis: Protect availability: the best ability is availability — gym work flexes around pitch load.
commonMistakes: stacking gym volume in congested weeks
dropping prevention work when fixtures compress

elite.trainingEmphasis: Individualised, monitored, minimal-dose development around a dense international calendar.
commonMistakes: ignoring accumulated trunk fatigue in camps

masters.trainingEmphasis: Retain power and tissue capacity; recover longer; keep playing.
commonMistakes: training like a 25-year-old on a 45-year-old recovery curve

offSeason.primaryObjective: Rebuild max strength, adductor/hamstring capacity and aerobic base; fix the season's asymmetries and niggles.
offSeason.trainingEmphasis: Max strength + hypertrophy where needed; eccentric/robustness work; aerobic base away from the stick.

preSeason.primaryObjective: Convert strength to acceleration/power; build RSA and interchange conditioning; re-expose to COD volume gradually.
preSeason.trainingEmphasis: Power + speed conversion; RSA blocks; adductor/COD progressions ahead of pressing volume.

competition.primaryObjective: Maintain qualities at minimal effective volume; maximise match availability.
competition.trainingEmphasis: 1-2 short heavy-but-low-volume sessions; prevention pillars every week; power micro-doses.
competition.intensity: high (low volume preserves quality without fatigue)

playoffs.trainingEmphasis: Minimal-volume high-intensity maintenance; priming; ruthless prioritisation.

recovery.primaryObjective: Physical and mental recovery; restore tissue; address carried niggles.
recovery.trainingEmphasis: Unstructured activity, mobility, light cross-training; rehab of the season's flags.

oneMatchPerWeek.pattern: MD-anchored; heavy gym early in the week, sharpen late.
oneMatchPerWeek.heavyDay: MD-4 or MD-3 (lower-body strength + trunk, far from the match)
oneMatchPerWeek.injuryPreventionDay: embedded daily; primary dose MD-4/MD-3 (Nordic, Copenhagen, calf)
oneMatchPerWeek.typicalLoadingPattern: MD+1 recovery → MD-4 high → MD-3 moderate → MD-2 power → MD-1 light priming → MD

twoMatchesPerWeek.pattern: Recovery-first: maintenance micro-doses only between matches.
twoMatchesPerWeek.powerDay: optional micro-dose if >72 h between matches
twoMatchesPerWeek.injuryPreventionDay: low-dose maintenance only (short Nordic + squeeze holds)
twoMatchesPerWeek.typicalLoadingPattern: Match → recovery → activation → Match → recovery; cut gym volume ~45%.

tournamentOrCongested.pattern: Tournament hockey (multi-match weekends, internationals) = pure availability management.
tournamentOrCongested.typicalLoadingPattern: Protect recovery between fixtures; gym is priming, never development.

transfersWell: hip hinge strength (posture protection + hit base)
limitedValue: slow bilateral-only programmes that ignore the lunge base
sit-up style trunk flexion (adds to the flexion the sport already imposes)
long steady-state gym cardio (pitch handles conditioning)
gymPhilosophy.singleLegEmphasis: Very high — the game lives on one leg in a lunge; single-leg strength and control outrank bilateral numbers.
gymPhilosophy.olympicLiftingSuitability: Optional — useful RFD tool if already technical; trap-bar jumps and med-ball work deliver most of the benefit at lower cost.
gymPhilosophy.plyometricEmphasis: Low-moderate and targeted: ankle stiffness + short-contact hops for COD; hockey's own running supplies most reactive load.
gymPhilosophy.coreTrainingPhilosophy: The trunk RESISTS: anti-flexion endurance to survive the crouch, anti-rotation strength to transmit hitting force. Never add loaded flexion to a sport made of flexion.
gymPhilosophy.gripTraining: Forearm endurance micro-doses support stick control late in matches.
gymPhilosophy.rotationalTraining: High value — med-ball rotational throws + cable rotations mirror hit/flick force transfer from a flexed base.
gymPhilosophy.isometricTraining: Valuable in-season: squeeze holds, calf isometrics and trunk holds maintain capacity at minimal fatigue.
gymPhilosophy.tempoRecommendations: Controlled eccentrics in robustness phases (hamstring, calf); explosive intent on all power work.
gymPhilosophy.velocityRecommendations: Heavy-fast intent for strength-speed; lighter loads at max intent for the first-step profile.

exercises.name: Trap-bar deadlift
exercises.jointLoading: moderate (spine-friendlier than straight bar — matters in a flexion-loaded sport)

exercises.name: Copenhagen adduction
exercises.secondaryAdaptation: groin-injury protection for the lunge-heavy game

exercises.name: Rear-foot-elevated split squat
exercises.primaryAdaptation: single-leg strength in the game's base position

exercises.name: Pallof press
exercises.secondaryAdaptation: lumbar protection under the flexed posture

exercises.name: Calf raise (straight + bent knee)
exercises.secondaryAdaptation: Achilles load tolerance for turf running

exercises.name: Pull-up
exercises.secondaryAdaptation: counterweight to the flexed playing posture

monitoringRecommendations: weekly Nordic force or bridge-hold check

injuryPreventionLibrary.recommendedFrequency: trunk endurance 2x/week all season; hip mobility daily micro-doses
monitoringRecommendations: track flick/hit volumes like sprint counts
injuryPreventionLibrary.source: Reilly & Seaton 1990; McGill (trunk endurance principles); expert consensus

exercisesToAvoid: sudden max-effort COD volume when flagged
reactive cutting volume immediately after a sprain
monitoringRecommendations: single-leg balance checks after any sprain

decisionRules.then: remove high-soreness gym work (Nordic to maintenance dose, heavy eccentrics, novel exercises); low-fatigue priming only
gym is CNS priming only (a few jumps/med-ball throws) or rest; no strength development
cut gym volume ~45%; maintenance micro-doses only; recovery leads
force a deload week: cap volume, protect availability, flag for review
rebuild gradually — one step down from planned load; no spikes

decisionRules.if: readiness score low (poor sleep + soreness + low wellness)
decisionRules.then: autoregulate down one step; quality over volume; do not test
treat as neuromuscular fatigue: reduce CNS-demanding work; recheck in 48 h
withhold training until symptom-free; resume gradually
reduce intensity one step on arrival days; mobility + easy work
hold strength at minimal effective volume (1-2 short heavy sessions/week); keep Nordic + Copenhagen + calf pillars

decisionRules.if: high hamstring soreness or Nordic strength drop
decisionRules.then: remove sprint work + heavy eccentric hamstring loading; isometric substitutes; flag

decisionRules.if: low-back soreness beyond normal training response
decisionRules.then: cut flexed-base rotation volume (hitting/flick pattern work) + heavy hinge loading; pain-free trunk endurance + hip mobility instead; flag
decisionRules.source: Reilly & Seaton 1990; McGill trunk principles; expert consensus

acwr.model: acute (7-day) : chronic (28-day) workload ratio; rolling/EWMA preferred
acwr.source: Gabbett 2016 — methodology contested; used as a conservative guardrail

loadManagement.weeklyProgressionGuideline: Avoid >~10-15% week-to-week spikes in running or hitting/flick volume; progress ONE stressor at a time (pitch, gym, or striking volume — never all three).

gymVolumeRanges.inSeason: low maintenance (1-2 sessions; ~6-10 hard sets/wk per region)

loadManagement.minimumEffectiveVolume: ~1 heavy low-volume session/week sustains strength in-season
loadManagement.maximumAdaptiveVolume: Off-season is the development window — push volume there, not in-season.
loadManagement.maximumRecoverableVolume: Constrained by pitch load + (usually) amateur/semi-pro life load; gym never compromises the next pitch session.
loadManagement.deloadRecommendations: Planned deload every 3-5 weeks in development phases; automatic deload on ACWR/readiness triggers.
loadManagement.progressionRules: Progress load when reps/quality are met at target RPE and readiness is green.
loadManagement.regressionRules: On red readiness or congested fixtures, drop one step (volume first, intensity second).
loadManagement.missedSessionRules: Never stack missed sessions; resume the planned wave.

thresholds.modifier: corroborating signal only — never sole driver

readinessModel.notes: Subjective wellness + sleep + prior load lead; objective signals corroborate. Raw vitals stay private to the athlete — the coach sees only the derived readiness state.

coachDashboard.principle: Coach sees DERIVED and availability signals only — never an individual's raw vitals (HRV, sleep, resting HR).
coachDashboard.trafficLightIndicators: Per-player green/amber/red from derived readiness + load state (never raw vitals).
coachDashboard.privacyNote: All per-athlete entries are DERIVED (readiness score, load state, availability). Raw HRV/sleep/RHR never appear on a coach surface — see TEAM-ARCHITECTURE data-isolation rules.

educationTips: why the crouch makes your hips and trunk the engine room
why Nordics and Copenhagens are non-negotiable pillars
why hitting volume counts like sprint volume for your back
why the best ability is availability

strongEvidence: Nordic hamstring programmes reduce hamstring injury (~50%, L1)
Copenhagen adduction reduces groin injury (~41%, L1)
subjective wellness is a sensitive readiness input (L1)
balance training reduces recurrent ankle sprain (L2)
weakEvidence: position-specific demand splits at club level
areasRequiringExpertJudgement: balancing pitch vs gym load in congested weeks
asymmetry management for the one-sided posture
areasRequiringFutureResearch: quarters-era match demands at club level
lumbar load quantification in the crouched posture
potentialRisksIfMisimplemented: adding loaded trunk flexion to an already flexion-loaded sport (low-back overload)
heavy posterior-chain work the day before sprint-dense sessions (hamstring risk)
treating the gym as conditioning (pitch already supplies it) — cumulative overload
copying football-code plyometric volumes (hockey needs less)
ignoring left-right asymmetry until it presents as injury
